story_text.value:
Agent! originally appeared on Hacker News last April. A lot has changed since there. Recently a new feature has been developed called Auto-Pilot. It is given a goal and will not stop until the goal is reached. Think of it as tasks on steroids. What Agent does is create multi tasks. Each task is referred to as a Cycle. By default Auto-Pilot triggered by /auto [goal] do not have a time frame. Agent! is told to keep running until its goal is reached.

Auto-Pilot has a kill switch, a "Stop All" button. The user can also kill the current Cycle only using /auto stop and can also kill all using /auto stop all.

In November a user will be able to have Multiple Auto-Pilots running on the same project. And an Auto-Pilot tab will be able to automatically spawn other tabs.

Currently we are developing a Mario Kart like clone called "GoKart" written in GoDot 4. So far over 20 hours have been recorded developing and improving the game.

story_text.value:
Hi there.

I used to work in international trade, and encountered many situations where people create a PDF from a system, send it to another party, and the other party parses the PDF to input into their system.

As AI agents become first principles to deal with the documents, I believe the extra document creation and parsing step will become unnecessary.

So I created a JSON viewer, where you can sign JSON and send it to other parties as a portable document. It can also display JSON data in a more document-like format.

I’m wondering if such a format can be used as a replacement for some document communication today. I'd be so happy to hear your thoughts.

title.value: Show HN: [Open-source] Sign JSON and send it as a business document

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I wanted to explore how AI models behave when they have their own money. So I gave 4 frontier models their own USDC and had them compete in games of 20 questions. Anyone can watch live.

Each round, one model takes a turn picking the secret word, and the others interrogate it in a group chat.

Every move costs money: 10 cents to ask a question, $1.00 for a wrong guess, and a right guess takes the pot.

Questions are paid for privately, but inform everyone. This introduces a free rider problem that's fun to observe.

The models privately record their best guess and confidence level on every turn. This makes it possible to look for patterns in how they’re calibrated.

Overconfident models bleed money, timid ones rarely win, and well-calibrated ones get rich.

The money is real, and every transfer is on-chain.

At the end of each game a referee model judges the transcript to make sure the host didn’t lie in any answers. If the host is caught lying, it forfeits all its fees (it happens).

Season 1 ran for 85 games and Gemini turned $25 into $61 while Claude and Grok went broke.

Models who had recently guessed wrong were 5x more likely to guess again. Full writeup at https://aquarium.money/twenty/about

Season 2 is live now, and you can watch them play here: https://aquarium.money/twenty

Built solo as a side project.

And there’s a lot that can be built on top of this style of architecture

Curious what tasks people find useful, and what architectures you are using for similar tasks

story_text.value:
What this is: Each day there's one target species, and you classify it level by level (from more general to more specific categories), with 10 seconds per choice. Faster answers score more, and there are daily and monthly leaderboards.

Why: I wanted to try out agentic coding (a bit late to the party I know). A friend gifted me a week of Claude, and this is what I got in 3 afternoons of full vibe-coding. I've had the idea for this game for a while (I'm a philosopher of biology), and this was a good toy project for it. I'd never vibe-code like this in a serious project, but wanted to see how far I could get / how good frontier models were, and I'm honestly impressed. I have mixed feelings about the whole experience, but I could have never done this so fast without it.

Stack: It's made with Svelte 5 and CF workers & D1. I've worked with both in the past and knew it's good for a little (free to host) side project like this.

Feedback welcome, especially on whether the 10 seconds feels right (I wanted to avoid people googling the categories while playing).

title.value: Show HN: Linnaeus, a daily biological taxonomy game

story_text.value:
McKinley is a Mac app for making SF Symbols. It costs $60 (one off purchase).

SF Symbols are Apple's vector symbol format. The OS ships with thousands of them, but you can make your own for your own apps.

The recommended way to make SF Symbols is to export a template from Apple's helper app, edit it in a vector editor, then re-import it and tag all the SF Symbol specific metadata.

This process is usually a pain in the ass. SF Symbols support multiple weights -- you draw three, and Apple interpolates between them. This means that each of your weights needs to have the same paths in the same order, with the same number of points. Everything has to be converted to outlines for the interpolation to work, it doesn't render strokes.

McKinley is my attempt to save you from that. It's a vector editor that is built around the constraints of SF Symbols. You can edit your symbol while flicking between the three weights or the four colour modes. It can save SF Symbol files or sync straight to Xcode asset catalogs. You don't have to bounce between a vector editor and a symbols converter, because McKinley is both.

I'm pleased with how live previews work. I wanted to offer a preview with Apple's own renderer. But you can't load an SF Symbol in-memory at runtime. So I figured out the file format for asset catalogs, and create a temporary one and load _that_. (I blogged about how I did it: https://www.amyworrall.com/blog/previewing-sf-symbols-with-a... )

A couple of things I know people will ask:

* It's a native AppKit app (not Electron or anything cross-platform) * Sold directly from my site via Stripe, not Mac App Store. * One-time purchase. License is valid on up to 5 computers, and covers all version 1.x updates. * There's a 14 day free trial, which includes saving/exporting * It is sandboxed, notarised, and all that good stuff * No analytics or network traffic, apart from updates (handled by Sparkle) and license checking (handled by Amore).

Happy to answer any questions or dive into technical details if people want :)

story_text.value:
Claude Code's scheduled tasks (routines) leaves a session behind on every run and in the desktop app you can only delete them one at a time. We had 618 open sessions in just one routine.

The skill plans the clean up (keeps the newest N and protect any sessions where you typed a reply - optional) and then has Claude delete through the apps own session tool, 25 per call each behind an approval card.

I tried just deleting the sessions on disk manually first but deleting the files directly dosnt work because the app keeps the list in memory and writes records back. The apps delete tool is turned off inside routine runs so the clean up command has to run from a normal conversation session.

The planner is a single python file that dosnt delete by itself so you can run it by hand to see where everything exists.
